'''Philippa Marrack,''' [[Royal Society|FRS]] (born 28 June 1945) is an English [[Immunology|immunologist]] and academic, based in the United States, best known for her research and discoveries pertaining to [[T cell]]s. Marrack is the Ida and Cecil Green Professor and chair of the Department of Biomedical Research at [[National Jewish Health]] and a distinguished professor of immunology and microbiology at the [[University of Colorado Denver]].<ref>{{Cite web|last=Williams|first=Brien|date=August 29, 2012|title=Oral History Project|url=https://www.aai.org/About/History/Past-Presidents-and-Officers/PhilippaMarrack|access-date= November 2, 2020|website=The American Association of Immunologists}}</ref>

==Biography==
Marrack was born in [[Ewell]], England on 28 June 1945.<ref>{{cite book|last=Yount|first=Lisa|title=A to Z of Women in Science and Math|year=2007|publisher=Infobase Pub.|location=New York|isbn=978-1-4381-0795-0|page=191|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=428i2UdWRRAC&pg=PA191 |edition=Rev.|chapter=Marrack, Philippa}}</ref><ref name="marquis">{{cite book |editor1-last=Marquis Who's Who |title=Marquis Who's Who |date=2016 |publisher=Marquis Who's Who LLC |edition=33rd |entry=Marrack, Philippa Charlotte}}</ref> Born in England, she maintains her British and American citizenship currently.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web|last=Emrich|first=John|date=2013|title=The American Association of Immunologists Oral History Project Transcript|url=https://www.aai.org/AAISite/media/About/History/OHP/Transcripts/Trans-Inv_012-Marrack_Philippa-2012_Final.pdf|access-date= November 2, 2020|website=The American Association of Immunologists}}</ref> Marrack's father served in the Royal Navy, so her family moved frequently throughout her childhood. Marrack notes that the longest she lived in one place during her early years was in Cambridge where she began pursuing her undergraduate degree.<ref name=":2" /> After attending [[University of Cambridge|Cambridge University]], Marrack moved to the United States to complete postdoctoral work and research. In the United States she met her lifelong partner and husband, [[John Kappler|John W. Kappler.]] They have completed much research and accomplished many advancements in the fields of immunology, biochemistry, and molecular biology.<ref name=":3">{{Cite web|title=Philippa Marrack, PhD|url=https://www.cogreatwomen.org/project/philippa-marrack-phd/|access-date=2020-11-02|website=Colorado Women's Hall of Fame|language=en-US}}</ref> Marrack and Kappler have two children together.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|title=Marrack, Philippa (1945–) Encyclopedia.com|url=https://www.encyclopedia.com/women/dictionaries-thesauruses-pictures-and-press-releases/marrack-philippa-1945|access-date=2020-11-02|website=www.encyclopedia.com}}</ref> Outside of science, Philippa Marrack enjoys playing the piano, as well as running along the Platte River with her Labradors.<ref name=":2" />

== Education ==
Marrack completed both undergraduate (1967) and Ph.D. (1970) at Cambridge University in [[New Hall, Cambridge]]. During her Ph.D., Marrack worked at the [[Cambridge MRC|MRC]] [[Laboratory of Molecular Biology]] with [[Alan Munro (immunologist)|Alan Munro]], where she began to study the differences between [[T cell]]s and [[B cell]]s. Alan Munro became her thesis advisor; she became the graduate student that worked with him due to his interest in working with a relative of John Marrack. [[John Marrack]] was Philippa Marrack's grandfather's brother, and a very well-known immunologist in the 1930s. Marrack notes that he indirectly influenced her to pursue the study of immunology.<ref name=":2" />

Marrack then moved to La Jolla, San Diego with her first husband and completed postdoctoral work with Richard Dutton at the [[University of California, San Diego]].<ref name=":4">{{Cite web|title=About NJ - Physician, Researcher or Clinician Detail - Philippa Marrack FRS, PhD - National Jewish Medical and Research Center|url=http://atopicderm.org/about/phys-fac/detail.aspx?doctorID=135|access-date=2020-11-02|website=atopicderm.org}}</ref> She credits Dutton as having a tremendous impact on her career during her fellowship, as he taught her how to write, lecture, and run a lab, as well as how to think critically.<ref name=":2" />

== Career ==
Marrack met her lifelong partner and current husband, [[John W. Kappler]], as a postdoctoral fellow at the [[University of California, San Diego]]. Her first faculty position was at the [[University of Rochester]], where she taught an undergraduate immunology course.<ref name=":4" /> The pair launched a joint lab at the [[University of Rochester]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Powell|first=Kendall|date=2004-12-01|title=Profile: Philippa Marrack|journal=Nature Medicine |language=en|volume=10|issue=12|pages=1270|doi=10.1038/nm1204-1270|pmid=15580239|s2cid=43191184|issn=1546-170X|doi-access=free}}</ref> At the same time, she received independent funding from the [[American Heart Association]] and [[American Cancer Society]] to study T cells. Marrack obtained an associate professorship at the University of Rochester, followed by faculty positions at the [[National Jewish Medical and Research Center|National Jewish Health]], Denver, Colorado and the [[University of Colorado Denver]]. She was also a [[Howard Hughes Medical Institute]] investigator.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://www.aai.org/About/History/Past-Presidents-and-Officers/PhilippaMarrack|title=Philippa Marrack, Ph.D.|website=American Association of Immunologists|access-date=29 January 2020}}</ref> Throughout her career, Marrack has published over 300 peer-reviewed journal articles. Her numerous citations and journal articles places her as the third most influential researcher in the nation and distinguishes her as top female researcher.<ref name=":3" />

== Research interests ==
In 1983, while working in the labs at the National Jewish Health in Denver, Colorado, Philippa Marrack and her husband and research partner, John Kappler, discovered and isolated the T cell receptor, together with Ellis Reinherz and [[James P. Allison|James Allison]]. Later in 1987 resulting from this research, Marrack discovered how the immune system is capable of molecular discrimination, as the human body can get rid of T cells that target the body's own tissues, destroying them in the [[thymus]] before they have a chance to cause problems, yet the body retains the cells that combat invaders. She learned that destructive cells that fail to be destroyed can cause [[autoimmune disease]]s like [[Type 1 diabetes]], [[Multiple sclerosis]], and [[lupus]]. This foundational work on immunological tolerance by Marrack and Kappler led to their later discovery in 1990 of [[superantigen]]s: powerful toxins that stimulate a large amounts of T-cell proliferation and can cause devastating immune response and violent symptoms such as those seen in [[toxic shock syndrome]] or [[Foodborne illness|food poisoning]].<ref name=":3" /><ref>{{Cite web|title=Philippa Marrack|url=https://www.rockefeller.edu/greengard-prize/recipients/marrack/|access-date=2020-11-02|website=Greengard Prize|language=en}}</ref> Marrack's current research projects focus on why certain autoimmune diseases, like lupus or Multiple sclerosis, are more prevalent in women than in men. Marrack and Kappler have recently discovered a population of [[B cell]]s that may account for some of this observation.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Marrack, Philippa|url=https://www.womenofthehall.org/inductee/philippa-marrack/|access-date=2020-11-02|website=National Women’s Hall of Fame|language=en-US}}</ref> Her pioneering and revolutionary work isolating the T-cell receptor and describing how T cells protect against infection, drive autoimmune and allergic diseases, and play a possible role in rejection of cancers, has contributed greatly to the current understanding of vaccines, HIV, and immune disorders in the medical field.

== Professional activities ==
Marrack has served on editorial boards and many scientific journals including [[Cell Journal|Cell]], [[Science (journal)|Science]], and the [[Journal of Immunology]]. She has also served on various boards and panels for the [[American Cancer Society]], the [[National Institutes of Health]], and the [[Burroughs Wellcome Fund|Burroughs Welcome Fund]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=Philippa Marrack to Be Honored for Lifetime Achievement in Immunology : Denver Nursing Star|url=http://www.denvernursingstar.com/newsletter/newsletter_view.asp?newsid=526&catid=73&active=0&mode=current|access-date=2020-11-02|website=www.denvernursingstar.com}}</ref> From 1986 to 2017, Marrack was a [[Howard Hughes Medical Institute]] investigator. From 1995 to 2002, Marrack served on the American Association of Immunologists Council and served as president of the [[American Association of Immunologists]] (AAI) from 2000 to 2001.<ref name=":0" /> She has been a member of the [[National Academy of Sciences]] in the United States since 1989, and a Fellow of the [[Royal Society]] in Great Britain since 1997. She is also the current Ida and Cecil Green professor and chair of the Department of Biomedical Research at [[National Jewish Health]] and a distinguished professor at the [[University of Colorado Denver]]. She joined the faculties of National Jewish Health and the University of Colorado Health Sciences Center in 1979.
